li.a: ABC News: 8 Children Dead in Japanese School Stabbing
The Guardian: Eight children die in Osaka school stabbing
World Socialist Web Site (German): Massaker an japanischen Schulkindern stellt Gesellschaft in Frage
Al Jazeera: Death sentence for Japan child killer
Human Rights in Japan: Extrajudicial, Summary or Arbitrary Executions
The Asahi Shimbun: 21 years after school stabbings, students pledge to cherish life
Adnkronos (Jiji Press): Memorial Held for Fatal Osaka School Attack 25 Years Ago

content.p: On the morning of 8 June 2001, a man walked into a primary school in Ikeda, a town outside Osaka in western Japan, and attacked children in their classrooms. Within about ten minutes, eight pupils were dead. The killings were, as the Guardian put it the next day, by far the worst seen at a Japanese school. TIME called it the worst mass killing of schoolchildren in the country's history.

The attacker, Mamoru Takuma, had a record of psychiatric treatment and a history of erratic, anti-social behaviour that, the Guardian reported, kept him from holding down a job. Al Jazeera wrote that the attack severely shook a national sense of security that had already been battered by a series of senseless crimes.

The Guardian reported that the attacker entered a ground-floor classroom through a verandah shortly after 10 a.m., during the gap between lessons. He lunged at three boys standing near a blackboard. Their classmates ran into the corridor and out to the playground. Witnesses told reporters that the attacker followed the children and stabbed several more before moving to other classrooms packed with pupils.

Pupils in other rooms first heard the attack over the school's public address system. One girl told the Guardian that the announcement was cut off by a scream and the sound of a desk going over. Others described classmates, some in bloodstained uniforms, lying on the floor as the children fled. Jiji Press later gave the time of the attack as 10:12 a.m.

Two teachers pinned the attacker down, and police arrived soon after. ABC News reported that several children had been slashed before the teachers stopped him. Some of the injured ran into a nearby supermarket, where staff laid them on pieces of cardboard and tried to stop the bleeding with towels. Distraught parents rushed to the school, many of them trying to reach their children on mobile phones.

Police and the press built a picture of Takuma's life in the days after the attack. He dropped out of high school and left the Air Force for reasons no source gave; TIME said he served two years and WSWS said one. He worked as a bus driver and then, in 1998, as a maintenance man at an elementary school in Osaka. In 1999 he was dismissed after he was accused of drugging the water used to make the staff's tea. TIME reported that four teachers were hospitalised. The Guardian said he had been dismissed after lacing a colleague's tea with drugs.

TIME reported that he was not prosecuted for the tea incident because a judge ruled that he was mentally incapable of taking responsibility for it. He was admitted to a psychiatric hospital and released after a few weeks. He later worked as a taxi driver until he lost that job after an alleged punch to a hotel employee, which left the employee with a broken nose, according to the Guardian. The Guardian's report put that punch in October of the year before the attack. WSWS reported that his wife filed for divorce in December 1997, nine months after the marriage began.

The Guardian reported that at the time of the attack Takuma was attending a psychiatric hospital as an outpatient and receiving treatment for schizophrenia. WSWS said he had been diagnosed with schizophrenia and had been admitted to psychiatric clinics three times. The Guardian also reported, citing local media, that he had taken ten times his daily dose of drugs before the attack. Police quoted him as saying that he had tried to kill himself several times and wanted to be put to death.

The number of people hurt is the figure on which the reports disagree most. Jiji Press and Al Jazeera give 13 children and two teachers. The Asahi Shimbun's report gives the same in its body text, though its summary says 15 others, including teachers. TIME wrote of 15 pupils and two teachers. The Guardian reported 19 other pupils injured, with two teachers also hurt, and ABC News reported 21 other people injured in its first-day story. ABC also said that two children were pronounced dead at the scene and six more died at hospital, and that six others were said to have serious injuries.

The Guardian's first-day report said that none of the injured pupils was thought to be in serious condition, although one teacher was in critical condition after emergency surgery. The Asahi Shimbun wrote later that some of the injured were seriously hurt. Given the differences, this account uses the figure that most of the agencies and papers gave, and it names the source where the others differ.

Takuma was indicted on charges of murder and attempted murder. Al Jazeera reported that he told an early hearing that he wanted to pay for the crime with his life. He pleaded guilty to the killings and to injuring 13 other children and two teachers, according to Al Jazeera. TIME quoted police as saying he told them, "If I killed children, I knew I would get the death penalty."

The Osaka District Court passed sentence in August 2003. Al Jazeera, reporting on 28 August, said the prosecutors had asked for the death penalty and had called the attack "a cruel and indiscriminate mass killing" and an act of revenge against society. Takuma was 39 at sentencing, according to Al Jazeera. When the judge ordered him to stand, he shouted that he would get the death penalty anyway and wanted to speak one last time. The judge ordered him kept out of the courtroom, so he was absent when the verdict was read. His lawyers said he was not afraid of death. The families of the children issued a statement saying that this meant the opposite.

The court had ruled that he had a personality disorder but that he was fully responsible for the crime, according to FIDH, which opposes the death penalty and reported the defence's argument that he was insane or weak-minded. After Takuma withdrew an appeal to the High Court, the sentence became final in September 2003, according to FIDH. Jiji Press said the sentence became final about a year before the execution.

Takuma was executed on 14 September 2004, according to FIDH. Jiji Press gives only the month, and the Asahi Shimbun says September 2004 without a day. FIDH reported that a second prisoner, Sueo Shimazaki, was executed the same day. A UN special rapporteur wrote to the Japanese government that Takuma was reportedly hanged on 14 September 2004, and noted that Japan did not confirm or deny the execution. FIDH said it opposed the execution, and that it opposes the death penalty whatever the gravity of the crime. Its account of the case is therefore not neutral, although its statement of the court dates matches the other reports.
content.h2: Debate about mental illness and school safety
content.p: The attack led to a wave of soul-searching in Japan. Al Jazeera reported that the crime prompted calls for stiffer laws on crimes committed by people with mental illness. Doctors had judged him fit to stand trial because he could tell right from wrong at the time of the attack, according to Al Jazeera. The Guardian quoted commentators who blamed outdated attitudes toward mental illness and the stigma of seeking help. WSWS argued that Japan's psychiatric care pushed patients out of clinics quickly, with drugs and little therapy.

Prime Minister Junichiro Koizumi said he was "very worried about our children" and promised to help the victims and to make schools safe. The education minister, Atsuko Toyama, said: "This should never have happened. Schools should be places where children can feel safe and secure." TIME reported that schools across Japan sent children home early and held emergency meetings with parents.

The school question was harder than the crime itself. Al Jazeera said the country argued over how to make schools safer while keeping them from becoming fortresses. Japanese schools had long prided themselves on being open to the surrounding community. TIME reported that, as of the week of the attack, schools like Ikeda Elementary were typically open and easy to enter.

On 8 June the school holds a memorial service, almost every year. The Asahi Shimbun reported on the 21st anniversary, when the school again held the service with its students and teachers. Bells on the cenotaph were rung shortly after 10 a.m., the time of the attack, while families and staff stood in silence in front of a monument with the names of the victims. Three sixth-graders spoke on behalf of the school and said they would continue to cherish the preciousness of people's lives.

On the 25th anniversary, on 8 June 2026, about 760 people attended the ceremony, including bereaved relatives, pupils and staff, according to Jiji Press. Eight bells were rung. The principal, Shinichi Arakawa, said that an increasing number of teachers did not know about the tragedy, and that the fading of memory was a setback for school safety efforts. In the afternoon, a lecture was given at the university's Kashiwara campus to students training to be teachers. A university associate professor, Hiromi Ueda, gave an outline of the incident and said the whole school had not been able to grasp the situation and deal with it systematically. A student who attended said she had learned the importance of preparing for unexpected situations every day.
